title: A Lost English "Ghost Village," Long Hidden Beneath One of England's Largest Reservoirs, Has Mysteriously Resurfaced
excerpt: The remains of a “lost” English village hidden beneath the waters of an English reservoir for more than half a century have resurfaced.
content:
The remains of a “lost” English village, hidden beneath the waters of an English reservoir for more than half a century, recently reappeared amid falling water levels this summer.

The small rural settlement, known as Nether Hambleton, resurfaced due to severe drought conditions impacting Europe, which have caused water levels to significantly drop, revealing stone foundations and other remnants of the long-concealed village.

Once part of the broader agricultural community near the River Gwash, the historic village was cleared during construction of what originally became known as the Empingham Reservoir, a significant engineering effort that helped secure additional water for the region.

Like many similar former communities in other parts of the world, such as those flooded by the Tennessee Valley Authority in rural Appalachia in the early 20th century, Nether Hambleton’s residents were relocated, their homes and farms destroyed, and more than 3,000 acres of the surrounding countryside became submerged and forgotten to time.

Construction of the reservoir was completed in 1976, although the project still required several more years to fill.

The nearby town of Upper Hambleton survived, since it was situated on higher ground.

While Nether Hambleton’s remains were lost beneath the artificial lake’s waters, not all of the signs of the former settlement were erased, and the remains of former foundations and stonework related to structures that once stood there remained hidden beneath the reservoir’s waters.

Now, due to the exceptionally low water levels occurring in Europe this summer, portions of the site have resurfaced, providing a rare look at the former landscape and the “lost” communities that once thrived there before Rutland Water was created.

Their reappearance also highlights the severity of drought conditions affecting the region.

“Drought conditions are worsening and will continue to do so until we see significant and sustained rainfall,” said Tony Grayling, strategic drought lead at the Environment Agency and chairman of the National Drought Group, as reported by Heritage Daily.

The reappearance of Nether Hambleton is just one of several archaeological discoveries that have resurfaced amid the recent droughts affecting Europe. Other examples include the unexpected discovery of an ancient cult object in the waters of the Danube near Dunaújváros in Hungary, and the resurfacing of portions of Constantine’s Bridge near Gigen, Bulgaria.
